name: Civilizing mission
summary: The civilizing mission holds that more advanced societies, above all those of Europe and later the United States, have a duty to rule and uplift less advanced peoples by spreading their education, law, religion, trade and technology. Rule is justified as temporary tutelage for the subjects' improvement, often alongside an explicit hierarchy of races or civilizations. Its two models are assimilation, remaking others in the colonizer's image, and a paternal protection of native society.
scope: The nineteenth and early twentieth century imperial doctrine as stated by Jules Ferry's 1884 speech to the French Chamber, Kipling's 'The White Man's Burden' (1899), Mill's liberal case for tutelage of 'barbarians' in On Liberty, and Macaulay's 1835 Minute on education in India. It excludes modern development or humanitarian-intervention discourse except where it is explicitly the same project. It carries no domestic programme, so most domestic answers are low-confidence inferences.

keyFigures.name: Jules Ferry
keyFigures.role: French premier who defended colonial expansion as the duty of superior races

keyFigures.name: Rudyard Kipling
keyFigures.role: Author of 'The White Man's Burden', the best-known British expression of the idea

keyFigures.name: John Stuart Mill
keyFigures.role: Liberal philosopher who defended tutelary rule over 'backward' societies

universal-healthcare.rationale: The ideology promoted public health abroad as a civilizing measure (s1) but has no settled domestic healthcare programme; adherents ranged from Victorian liberals to republicans to conservatives.

raise-minimum-wage.rationale: Nothing in the civilizing-mission case addresses wage floors; adherents' views followed their home party, so the answer is split.

markets-allocate-better.rationale: Ferry sought export markets and Mill-style liberalism favoured trade, but the doctrine itself is about tutelage, so this is an inference from its commercial backers.

public-ownership.rationale: Imperial adherents defended private commerce and colonial enterprise; no source advances public ownership of utilities, so a mild inference against.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: The doctrine is silent on domestic taxation; adherents came from both propertied conservative and reformist republican camps.

unions-good.rationale: No stated position; colonial-era adherents split between paternalist reformers and employers' interests.

property-fundamental.rationale: Mill-era liberal imperialism assumed secure property as a mark of civilization, but this is inferred rather than stated in the sources.

regulate-corporations.rationale: Ferry saw colonies as outlets for industry, yet the doctrine takes no position on regulating firms at home.

cut-welfare.rationale: Not addressed; paternalist improvement ideas cut both ways, since uplift of 'dependants' could justify aid or self-reliance.

worker-ownership.rationale: Not addressed; commercial and industrial backers of empire (s2) would have opposed collective worker ownership.

surveillance-ok.rationale: No documented position on counter-terror surveillance; the doctrine predates it.

legalize-drugs.rationale: Inferred from the moral-improvement aim and Victorian respectability that adherents would restrict drugs; weakly evidenced.

restrict-hate-speech.rationale: Mill's liberalism opposes legal speech restrictions among the civilised; inferred, as the doctrine is about empire.

strong-leader.rationale: Mill and Ferry worked within parliamentary government at home; despotism is justified only over 'barbarians' (s4), not for the home polity.

limit-guns.rationale: Not addressed; adherents split by national tradition (British, French, American).

empower-police-military.rationale: Ferry stressed naval power and garrisons to hold colonies (s2); domestic police funding is inferred.

legalize-sex-work.rationale: Inferred from the moral-reform emphasis of missionary and Victorian civilizing projects; no direct source.

decide-locally.rationale: Macaulay and Ferry favoured policy set by a central metropolitan authority; local self-direction is the opposite of tutelage.

rehabilitation.rationale: Mill's improvement ideal and the reformist aim of 'bringing improvement' suggest rehabilitative sympathies, though not stated for prisons.

traditional-family.rationale: Civilizing projects exported Christian family norms (s1 notes divorce law reform in Puerto Rico to instil US norms), but views on home family structure are inferred.

same-sex-marriage.rationale: Historic adherents were socially conservative; some modern commentators note pro-LGBT rhetoric used in a new civilizing mission (s1), so strands differ.

abortion-legal.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from Christian missionary and Victorian moral norms.

more-religion-public.rationale: Christian evangelization was a stated aim (s1), though Ferry was a secularist, so adherents are mixed and the answer is inferred.

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Ferry and Kipling treated racial hierarchy as a fact justifying rule; acting to correct 'historical racial injustice' runs against it, but modern strands differ.

gender-social-construct.rationale: No stated position; adherents held conventional views of natural sex roles.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Ferry tied colonial expansion to national grandeur and decline avoidance (s2), and Kipling speaks of service to one's own people's standing; national pride is central.

gradual-change.rationale: Mill treats improvement as a staged process and tutelage as lasting only until peoples are capable of free discussion (s4); Kipling's burden is long and slow.

reduce-immigration.rationale: Not addressed; empire built on movement of Europeans abroad, not on immigration debates at home.

empower-international-orgs.rationale: Ferry's case relies on national sovereign action by powers; later UN-style bodies would oppose colonial rule, so an inference.

free-trade.rationale: Ferry wanted protected colonial markets against tariff walls (s2) while British adherents favoured free trade; adherents genuinely split.

nation-first.rationale: Ferry argued colonies were needed for France's rank, markets and naval security (s2), placing national interest first.

humanitarian-intervention.rationale: The doctrine is itself a moral justification for military intervention abroad (s1), and Kipling casts it as service to those guarded (s3).

open-borders.rationale: Imperial powers claimed rights over others' territory while holding their own borders; no source supports open borders.

limit-growth.rationale: Ferry's argument is that stagnation is decadence and growth needs outlets (s2); environmental limits were not discussed.

drastic-climate-action.rationale: Anachronistic; no basis in the sources.

tech-solves-problems.rationale: Roads, railways, dams and public health were stated aims of the mission (s1), reflecting faith in technical progress as improvement.

expand-nuclear.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the faith in modernization and large infrastructure that s1 records.

revolution-justified.rationale: Kipling and Ferry stood for imposed order; colonial resistance is portrayed as sullen ingratitude (s3).

experts-over-public.rationale: Mill allows despotism to guide those not yet capable of free discussion (s4) and Macaulay would train an educated intermediary class (s5); expert guidance is central.

central-planning.rationale: Not addressed; commercial and liberal supporters of empire favoured markets.

socialized-markets.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from the private-enterprise basis of colonial commerce.

land-value-tax.rationale: Mill discussed land taxation in other works but it is unrelated to the civilizing doctrine; no stated position.

tax-inheritance.rationale: Not addressed in the sources; adherents differ.

basic-income.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from Victorian ideas of improvement through work.

tariffs-protect-industry.rationale: Ferry cited foreign tariff barriers as reason to seek colonial outlets (s2) but British adherents were free traders; split.

state-directs-investment.rationale: Ferry urged state action to build ports, supply stations and colonial development (s2); strategic direction is inferred.

abolish-money-wages.rationale: The doctrine rests on trade, markets and commercial development (s1,s2); abolishing money and wage labour is foreign to it.

abolish-central-banks.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from conventional establishment finance.

corporatist-bargaining.rationale: No stated position; liberal and republican adherents did not favour state-recognised corporate bodies.

one-party-rule.rationale: Mill and Ferry were parliamentarians; Mill reserved despotism only for 'barbarians' (s4).

monarchy-legitimate.rationale: Kipling's Britain was monarchic and Ferry's France republican; the doctrine is indifferent to regime form at home.

democracy-best.rationale: Mill considered representative government ideal for advanced peoples but open to abuse, and denied it to the unprepared (s4); 'even when voters choose badly' is untested.

direct-votes.rationale: Mill favoured representative rather than direct government; inferred.

workers-councils.rationale: Workers' councils as a basis of power are alien to the elite-led, state-driven doctrine documented in s2 and s5.

right-to-secede.rationale: Ferry said France would 'never leave' its colonies (s2); secession would end the mission.

natural-rulers.rationale: The core claim is that some peoples are better placed to rule others for a time (s2,s4); the claim concerns advanced societies more than innate individual traits.

political-violence-never.rationale: Kipling praises the 'savage wars of peace' (s3) and Ferry defends conquest, so adherents accepted state violence for the mission; domestic political violence, the statement's main sense, is not discussed.

war-builds-character.rationale: Kipling stresses sacrifice and bloodshed in service of the burden (s3), but humanitarian strands would deny war's value; split.

separate-church-state.rationale: Ferry was an anticlerical secularist (s2 intro) while missionary strands wanted Christianity spread (s1); split.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Even missionary strands imposed European law rather than scripture-based law, and Ferry was secularist; inferred.

private-courts-defense.rationale: Ferry demanded state naval and military power (s2); private defence is contrary.

military-superiority.rationale: Ferry's case rests on naval bases and the ability to hold territory against rivals (s2).

ethnic-nation.rationale: The assimilation model aims to make peoples 'like us' (s1) rather than keep nations ethnically homogeneous; however racial-hierarchy thinking pulls the other way.

class-struggle-history.rationale: The doctrine sees history as civilizational progress led by advanced peoples (s1,s4), not class conflict.

equal-outcomes.rationale: Inferred; improvement is opportunity-based and hierarchical in the sources.

indigenous-land-authority.rationale: Colonization displaced indigenous authority in the name of bringing 'civility' and settled government (s1 cites the 1606 Virginia charter).

colonial-reparations.rationale: Ferry says Europe acquits itself of a duty with 'generosity' (s2); an adherent regards colonial rule as a benefit, not a debt.

civilizational-union.rationale: The mission posits the West as the carrier of civilization over others; unions of non-Western civilizations oppose it, while Western unity is not explicitly stated.

self-interest-moral.rationale: Kipling frames the burden as sacrifice and service, 'the best ye breed' sent out for others (s3), against self-interest as virtue.

duties-before-rights.rationale: The mission is posed as a duty (Ferry: 'right because they have a duty'; Kipling's 'burden'), a language of duty over rights.

industrial-civilization-disaster.rationale: Railways, industry and technology were central to the mission's idea of progress (s1), the reverse of the statement; anti-industrial critique is not discussed directly.

accelerate-technology.rationale: Adherents valued technical progress but also gradual, ordered change; no stated view on disruptive acceleration.

restore-past-order.rationale: The mission is a progress doctrine, with the West at the head of linear development (s1), not a restoration of a lost order.

results-over-ideology.rationale: Adherents defended the mission both by principle (duty) and by results (infrastructure, health); no clear position.

direct-action.rationale: Kipling and Ferry stand for established order and state action rather than direct action against it.

means-match-ends.rationale: The doctrine justifies coercive means (despotism, 'savage wars') for the sake of improvement (s3,s4), rejecting a match between means and ends.

return-to-foraging.rationale: Foraging societies were the very sort of 'primitive' life the mission aimed to leave behind (s1).

abolish-division-of-labor.rationale: The division of labour is never discussed; rejection is inferred from the mission's emphasis on trade, schooling and infrastructure.

distribute-by-need.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from market-oriented imperial commerce.

production-for-use.rationale: Ferry's argument is explicitly about industrial export markets and profit (s2).

profit-exploitation.rationale: Ferry defends colonial commerce as beneficial and necessary (s2); the Marxist exploitation thesis is a critic's claim.

dictatorship-of-proletariat.rationale: Alien to the elite-led metropolitan doctrine documented in s2 and s5.

collective-farming.rationale: Not addressed; colonial agriculture was plantation or smallholder-based.

capitalism-causes-war.rationale: Ferry presents colonial expansion as a duty and a solution to economic difficulty (s2), not as a cause of great-power war.

taxation-theft.rationale: Ferry's argument depends on state spending on fleets and colonies (s2), so taxation is legitimate.

harm-principle.rationale: Mill's harm principle is for civilised adults only; he exempts 'barbarians', so adherents apply it at home but not abroad (s4).

individual-rights-only.rationale: Ferry grounds rights in duties and in group rank ('superior races', s2); evidence thin on group rights.

conscription.rationale: Not addressed; Ferry's France had conscription while Britain did not.

exit-over-voice.rationale: Mill and Ferry treat government as a means to improvement; exit as an alternative to voting is unaddressed and contrary to tutelage.

state-as-business.rationale: Ferry saw the state as the strategic agent of national duty and rank (s2), not as a business.

positive-liberty.rationale: Mill's improvement ideal holds freedom is a capacity developed through education, and the mission claims to supply this capacity (s1,s4); inferred.

media-academia-power.rationale: The sources never discuss the relative power of universities, press and elected officials; adherents were themselves established elites, so no clear lean.

hereditarian-race.rationale: Ferry speaks of 'superior' and 'inferior' races (s2); many adherents saw hierarchy as cultural or stage-based rather than genetic, so only a weak yes.

organic-representation.rationale: Mill defended representative government through parties and elections; inferred.

total-state.rationale: Mill's liberal strand and Ferry's republic did not want a state directing culture and economy at home.

national-rebirth.rationale: Ferry warned of decadence from abstention (s2), but the doctrine's remedy is outward expansion rather than radical national rebirth; mixed.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Ferry explicitly calls for taking Tunisia, Indochina and Madagascar and warns that abstention is decadence (s2).

personal-loyalty-rule.rationale: Feudal oaths of loyalty conflict with the modern bureaucratic and parliamentary states of the doctrine's adherents.

bound-labor.rationale: Ferry condemns Spanish introduction of slavery as failing the duty of a higher race (s2); the mission's moral claim opposed bonded labour, though colonial forced labour existed in practice.

no-neutral-knowledge.rationale: Macaulay held that European learning simply outweighs native literature (s5); knowledge is not a mere reflection of power.

universal-morality.rationale: The mission presupposes a standard of civilization applicable to all peoples and discoverable by reason, as in Mill's progressive improvement (s4).

single-common-good.rationale: Mill pluralism at home versus a paternal single standard for tutelage abroad; split.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: Zionism lies outside the civilizing-mission sources; Ferry, Kipling, Mill and Macaulay say nothing on a Jewish state, so this is a neutral placeholder.

diaspora-return-right.rationale: None of the cited texts concerns diasporas or return rights; adherents have no shared position and the doctrine concerns rule over others.

revive-national-language.rationale: Macaulay's policy privileged English over native languages as vehicle of improvement (s5); revival of indigenous languages was not a goal.

workplace-democracy.rationale: Not addressed; inferred from commercial backing.

school-vouchers.rationale: The mission valued education (s1,s5) but no stance on vouchers.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Not addressed; Ferry also argued for state spending on colonial infrastructure.

economic-freedom.rationale: Mill-style liberal imperialism tied freedom and commerce, but this is inferred.

rule-by-example.rationale: Kipling sends 'the best ye breed' to serve, an appeal to the moral example and character of the rulers (s3), though coercion is also accepted.

national-self-determination.rationale: Self-government is withheld from peoples judged unprepared (s4); Ferry denies it to 'inferior races' (s2).

force-without-un.rationale: Ferry acts on national initiative without international authorisation (s2); UN approval is anachronistic.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Enlightenment progress is central, yet Christian evangelization was also a stated aim (s1); split.

welfare-for-citizens.rationale: The doctrine concerns duties toward subject peoples, not welfare eligibility of immigrants, so adherents follow their own home parties and split.

work-for-welfare.rationale: Inferred from Victorian improvement ethics; no source states it.

class-collaboration.rationale: The civilizing mission assumes harmony of a paternal elite and those it leads; inference for domestic class relations.

sacrifice-heritage.rationale: Macaulay prized European libraries and learning, and the mission sees cultural heritage as the foundation of civilization; wrecking it is contrary.

dominated-front.rationale: Common fronts against Western powers contradict the claim of Western rightful leadership (s2).

workers-nation.rationale: The mission's texts do not address how workers should organize; Ferry's appeal to national rank hints nationally, but no source states it.

distinct-gender-roles.rationale: Inferred; adherents held conventional gender roles.

ban-interest.rationale: Colonial commerce and finance (s2) are interest-based; a ban is foreign to it.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: The doctrine posits a racial hierarchy (s2) but its assimilationist wing (s1, Macaulay) aims at creating a mixed intermediary class; colonial practice varied.

state-class-instrument.rationale: A Marxist claim opposed to the mission's framing of the state as a moral agent of duty (s2).

expand-fossil-fuels.rationale: Ferry's concern for coal supply stations (s2) hints at energy focus, but position is inferred.

assimilate-immigrants.rationale: Assimilation, making peoples more like the rulers, is the mission's central model (s1) and Macaulay sought English taste and morals (s5); applied to immigrants by inference.

elite-replacement.rationale: A conspiracy theory with no place in the doctrine or its sources.

proportional-representation.rationale: Mill backed proportional representation in other works, but the doctrine itself is silent.

national-mission.rationale: This is the doctrine itself: nations such as France, Britain and the US held a duty to spread civilization and government to others (s1,s2).

patriarchy-structural.rationale: Not addressed; adherents of the period would have denied a structural patriarchy.

political-elite-corrupt.rationale: Adherents were themselves political elites; Ferry was a premier.

heritable-defect-limits.rationale: Not addressed; eugenics was popular among some but not a part of the doctrine.

security-forces-accountable.rationale: Kipling presents the 'dead' and the wars of peace as the price of the burden (s3); prosecuting abuses by one's own forces is contrary.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Ferry wanted an active state for colonies and education.

discourage-race-mixing.rationale: Racial-hierarchy thinking suggests discouragement, assimilationism suggests otherwise; adherents split.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Ferry's 'superior' and 'inferior' races and Kipling's 'half-devil and half-child' (s2,s3) deny equality of status, even where the mission aims to raise others.

socialism-one-country.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist debate with no bearing on a doctrine of imperial tutelage; adherents did not take a side.

settler-state-colonial.rationale: Settlement was justified as bringing civility and settled government (s1); calling it a colonial project is the critic's frame, though adherents themselves used 'colony'.

uniform-civil-code.rationale: Macaulay's reform legal project aimed at common codes (s5); inferred as to religion.

restrict-conversion.rationale: Missionary strands sought conversion (s1), so restricting it would be opposed.

ban-cattle-slaughter.rationale: Macaulay dismissed native religious learning as error (s5); inferred.

no-religion-state-schools.rationale: Ferry secularized French education (s2 intro) but missionary education was a stated aim (s1); split.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Mill holds despotism legitimate over barbarians for their improvement (s4), so consent is not the sole basis of legitimacy.

trade-surplus.rationale: Ferry's search for export outlets (s2) suggests a mercantile attitude.

population-transfer.rationale: Not a stated aim; assimilation rather than expulsion is the model (s1).

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Kipling's 'savage wars of peace' and Ferry's conquest policy treat initiating force as acceptable for the end of civilizing (s2,s3).

competition-drives-progress.rationale: Ferry frames rivalry among powers as reason to act (s2) while humanitarian strands stress duty over competition; split.

ban-extremist-parties.rationale: Nothing in Ferry, Kipling, Mill or Macaulay addresses outlawing parties; Mill's liberalism and republican defence of the regime pull in opposite directions.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Mill's despotism over barbarians (s4) allows domination for improvement; inferred.

separated-powers.rationale: Not addressed beyond conventional parliamentary views.

vanguard-party.rationale: The doctrine has its own tutelary vanguard of a metropolitan elite (s5), but not a revolutionary party.

priority-to-poor.rationale: The burden is service to the less fortunate abroad (s3), but no domestic priority is stated.

restrict-strikes-picketing.rationale: Strike law was not discussed by the mission's proponents, and Ferry's republicans and Victorian conservatives differed on it.

population-causes-poverty.rationale: The sources attribute backwardness to lack of civilization and education, not to population growth, but no passage tests this claim directly.

diversity-weakens-cohesion.rationale: Not addressed; assimilationist strands implied mixed views.

offices-by-lottery.rationale: The doctrine rests on competent guidance of the less prepared (s4); lottery is contrary.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Kipling and Ferry accept extraordinary measures in the service of order (s3); inferred.

price-controls-essentials.rationale: Not discussed; liberal adherents like Mill favoured markets, while paternal administrators sometimes fixed colonial food prices, so neutral.

party-controls-media.rationale: Mill's liberalism opposes state control of the press at home.

party-commands-army.rationale: Ferry's republic had state commanded forces; inferred.

long-naturalization-wait.rationale: Citizenship timing is outside the doctrine; assimilationists would favour quick integration while hierarchical views favour delay, leaving no clear lean.

representatives-worker-pay.rationale: Not addressed; Mill opposed paying representatives mean wages.

party-discipline-binding.rationale: Party rules for legislators are not discussed by any source for this doctrine, and adherents sat in parties of many kinds.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Ferry's nationalist imperial standpoint (s2) favours national sovereignty; inferred.

church-by-bishops.rationale: Church governance is not part of the doctrine; Anglican and Catholic missions favoured bishops, while Ferry's secular republic stood apart, so adherents split.

clerical-rule.rationale: Ferry was the champion of anticlerical laws (s2 intro), and Mill-style liberalism rejects clerical rule.

defeat-own-government-war.rationale: Adherents treated the nation's work abroad as a patriotic duty (s2, s3), which rules out working for one's own government's defeat; revolutionary defeatism is not discussed directly.

censor-art-for-virtue.rationale: The doctrine speaks of moral improvement of subject peoples but never of censoring art; Mill's liberal strand opposes it, others would allow it.

unlimited-reelection.rationale: Presidential term limits are not discussed in any source; republican and monarchical adherents had different habits.

recall-officials.rationale: Recall of officials is not addressed; Mill preferred representatives using their own judgment, but the doctrine itself takes no side.

end-foreign-alliances.rationale: Ferry says France will 'never leave' its colonies and bases (s2); withdrawing troops from abroad is the opposite.

abolish-rental-housing.rationale: Foreign to the doctrine and to property-respecting adherents.

people-in-arms.rationale: Ferry favoured a naval and standing military force for expansion (s2).

rural-life-healthier.rationale: The mission built towns, railways and ports (s1) and judges rural life as less advanced.

educated-out-of-touch.rationale: Macaulay's policy is to build a learned class as intermediaries (s5); disdain for the educated is contrary.

cultures-equal-different.rationale: The doctrine holds some civilizations higher than others: Ferry's 'superior' races (s2) and Macaulay's single shelf outweighing native literature (s5).

death-penalty.rationale: Inferred from Victorian-era establishment practice and the willingness to use force for order.

sex-ed-in-schools.rationale: Anachronistic; the sources do not address it.

creationism-in-schools.rationale: Macaulay prized European science over native 'false astronomy' (s5), so teaching creationism is contrary.

restrict-pornography.rationale: Inferred from Victorian moral reform and missionary norms.

citizenship-by-descent.rationale: Not addressed; the assimilation model (s1) points the other way, imperial nationality varied.

minority-language-support.rationale: Macaulay favoured English over native languages (s5); assimilation required replacing them.

religious-exemptions.rationale: Macaulay's common legal codes (s5) leave less room for exemptions; inferred.

encourage-eccentricity.rationale: Mill favoured eccentricity for civilised people in On Liberty (s4), but other adherents were conformist; split.

independence-needs-economic-change.rationale: The doctrine denies independence is on the agenda for the colonised; the Marxist thesis is a critic's.

constituent-assembly.rationale: How constitutions are rewritten is not discussed in the sources; adherents served established regimes and had no common view.

restrict-freedoms-for-growth.rationale: Mill says despotism is legitimate to improve barbarians (s4), a temporary restriction of freedom for development.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Kipling's burden is a duty of the advanced to serve the poor and backward (s3), though the stated aim is rule rather than aid.

independent-nuclear-deterrent.rationale: Anachronistic; Ferry's call for national military power suggests it.

direct-election-head-of-state.rationale: Method of choosing a head of state is unrelated to the mission; British monarchists and French republicans both held the doctrine.

central-bank-independence.rationale: Anachronistic for nineteenth-century imperialists, and the sources contain no monetary doctrine, so neutral.

no-land-for-peace.rationale: Ferry's refusal to leave acquired places (s2) suggests no retreat of territory; inferred.

property-serves-common-good.rationale: Mill allowed regulating property in other works; not addressed by the doctrine.

precautionary-principle.rationale: Anachronistic; the sources show faith in confident technical improvement but say nothing on environmental risk under uncertainty.

collective-defense.rationale: Imperial powers allied and defended each other's colonies; inferred.

annexed-territory-occupation.rationale: Annexation without consent of the people is how the mission operated (s1); such territory is not held unlawful.

subordinate-church-to-state.rationale: Ferry did curb Church power in schools (s2 intro), missionary strands did not; split.

nonpartisan-head-of-state.rationale: Whether the head of state stands above parties is not part of the doctrine, which was held under both monarchy and republic.

force-to-prevent-secession.rationale: Ferry's refusal to leave acquired territories (s2) implies force to retain them.

region-keeps-system.rationale: The assimilationist model replaces local systems (s1); the associationist model differs.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Not a feature of the doctrine.

flat-income-tax.rationale: Tax structure is not discussed in any consulted source, and adherents from different parties disagreed.

character-from-environment.rationale: Macaulay's project assumes that education can remake Indian minds into 'English in taste' (s5); Mill's improvement also assumes malleability (s4).

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Mill's despotism is justified by its end (s4) but still accountable to improvement; at home adherents accepted rule of law.

space-expansion.rationale: Anachronistic; Ferry's expansion argument concerns Earth territory and markets, so no stance on space can be drawn.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Not addressed; Mill favoured representative government with safeguards.

equal-parenting.rationale: Anachronistic family-court issue never addressed by the mission's proponents, so neutral.

class-struggle-under-socialism.rationale: Presupposes socialist states, which the doctrine's adherents did not discuss, so no position can be derived.

land-redistribution.rationale: Colonization itself took land under settled government (s1); redistribution to cultivators was not a goal, though some reform schemes existed.

refugee-return.rationale: Not discussed in the sources; the doctrine concerns ruling others, not return rights after conflict.

co-ethnic-territorial-claim.rationale: Not addressed; claims based on civilizing or settlers differ.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Missionary strands sought conversion (s1); punishing leaving religion contradicts liberal and missionary aims.

women-must-cover.rationale: Women's dress codes were seen as backwardness; later versions of the mission cite women's rights as justification (s1).

common-currency.rationale: Monetary union is not addressed; adherents were nation-state imperialists but had no stated view of shared currencies.

kin-peoples-union.rationale: Not addressed; adherents tied to nation-states and empires.

national-cultural-autonomy.rationale: Macaulay and Ferry's assimilationism opposes separate self-governing cultural institutions (s1,s5).

rights-where-you-live.rationale: The question is about persecuted minorities choosing between emigration and local equal rights; the doctrine offers no guidance.

material-conditions-drive-history.rationale: Mill and the progress thinkers (s1) emphasize ideas and education as the engine of progress.

ban-cartels.rationale: Competition policy is not addressed; liberal free-traders and protectionist adherents differed.

no-bailouts.rationale: Bailouts are not discussed by the sources and adherents had no shared view, so neutral.

courts-bound-by-majority.rationale: Mill feared the tyranny of majorities; inferred.

economic-self-sufficiency.rationale: Ferry sought colonial markets (s2) in a protected bloc, but British adherents were free traders; split.

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: Anachronistic; trade-agreement standards did not exist, and the doctrine takes no stance on them.

armed-group-creates-revolution.rationale: Adherents defend order; revolution is portrayed as ingratitude (s3).

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Not addressed; republicans and monarchists both adhered.

history-own-civilization.rationale: Macaulay's policy centred European learning (s5) and the mission sees European civilization as the standard (s1).

civilizing-tutelage.rationale: Stated explicitly: Ferry says superior races have a duty to civilize inferior ones (s2); Mill says despotism is legitimate for barbarians if the end is their improvement (s4).

patriotic-education.rationale: Ferry built the French republican school system around civic and national loyalty (s2 intro).

end-racial-preferences.rationale: Modern admissions policy is outside the doctrine, and modern strands of the label are contested, so neutral.

capitalism-adapts.rationale: Ferry sees colonial markets as solving an economic difficulty (s2), implying capitalism can adapt.

former-empire-influence.rationale: Continued cultural influence in former colonies (Francophonie, Lusotropicalism) is documented as a continuation of the mission (s1).

delink-world-market.rationale: The mission integrates others into trade; delinking is rejected (s1,s2).

labor-aristocracy.rationale: A Marxist thesis rejected by those who view colonial gains as shared benefits.

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Entrenched rights charters are not discussed; Mill's concern for individual liberty and parliamentary adherents' views conflict.

colonial-treaties-void.rationale: Ferry's case rests on acquiring and holding colonial territory (s2); voiding the treaties and divisions is contrary.

elective-rulers.rationale: Regime form at home varied; Mill held elected rulers suit advanced peoples.

minority-veto.rationale: Mill reserves tutelage for the unprepared and allows rule over dissent (s4); minority veto is contrary.

resist-lawless-ruler.rationale: Mill allowed resistance in civilised states but denied it where tutelage applied; split.

parliament-supreme.rationale: Parliamentary supremacy is not part of the doctrine; British and French adherents likely agreed but monarchists differed.

animal-suffering-matters.rationale: Mill's utilitarianism counted animal suffering but the doctrine does not address it.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Kipling casts empire as the duty of the privileged to those they guard (s3); noblesse oblige is its domestic analogue.

withdraw-from-politics.rationale: Kipling's 'White Man's Burden' (s3) demands active public service and sacrifice for the mission, the opposite of withdrawal; the good-life claim is not discussed directly.

ruling-class-consent.rationale: This Gramscian thesis is a critic's analysis; the sources say nothing on how elites win consent, so no position is stated.

world-economy-extracts-surplus.rationale: Dependency thesis is the critic's view; Ferry says Europe brings benefits (s2).

native-born-offices.rationale: Macaulay's intermediaries are native-born in the colonies, but the doctrine is silent on restricting offices.

party-own-road.rationale: A Marxist-Leninist question outside the doctrine of imperial tutelage.

self-reliance-over-aid.rationale: The mission has the advanced guiding and supplying the less advanced (s3), against reliance on local resources.

return-lost-territory.rationale: Revanchism is not part of the mission; Ferry's France lost Alsace-Lorraine, but his speech turns attention to colonies, so adherents split.

indigenous-political-leadership.rationale: The mission puts rule in the hands of the advanced (s2), not descendants of the pre-colonial peoples.

antifascism-founding-value.rationale: Anachronistic for the nineteenth-century doctrine, and modern strands are contested.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Anachronistic; the doctrine's sources predate both ideologies and give no basis for an answer.

slavery-not-civil-war-cause.rationale: US Civil War causes are unaddressed by the sources; Ferry did condemn slavery, but this does not decide the historical question.

preserve-contested-monuments.rationale: Inferred; defenders of imperial legacy generally resist removal.

male-disadvantage-attention.rationale: Anachronistic gender-policy issue not addressed by the doctrine, so neutral.

domestic-violence-symmetry.rationale: Anachronistic and not addressed by any consulted source, so neutral.

institutions-fit-civilization.rationale: Mill held that representative government does not suit peoples at a 'barbarous' stage (s4), but as a stage to grow out of under European tutelage, not as a licence for their own forms; Ferry and Macaulay's assimilationism rejects the statement outright, while associationists kept native forms; mild disagreement is contested across strands.

paid-care-work.rationale: Anachronistic and not addressed in the sources, so neutral.

office-by-exam.rationale: Macaulay's colonial reforms favoured educated competitive service (s5).

foreign-takeover-block.rationale: The mission's backers were commercial powers that wanted open investment abroad, yet governments also protected strategic firms, so adherents split.

no-fault-divorce.rationale: s1 notes US legalizing divorce in Puerto Rico as an instance of social reform, but adherents split at home.

recallable-delegates.rationale: Mill favoured representatives using judgment rather than being bound.

individual-pension-accounts.rationale: Pension design is not discussed by the doctrine, and its adherents had no shared view.

land-use-tenure.rationale: Colonization often sought formal private title for civilization (s1); inferred.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Inferred from parliamentary regimes of adherents.

reunify-divided-nation.rationale: The doctrine says nothing on borders drawn by outside powers; imperial powers themselves drew such borders, but adherents had no reunification programme.

state-harmful.rationale: The mission was carried out through state fleets, garrisons and administration (s2), so its adherents plainly did not see the state as harmful; anarchism is not discussed.

single-official-language.rationale: Macaulay's Minute made English the medium of colonial education, though it concerned schooling more than every area of public life.

foreign-land-ownership.rationale: Colonial rule involved settlers, concessions and European ownership of land abroad, so excluding foreigners from land is contrary to the project; inferred.

disparate-impact-discrimination.rationale: The doctrine rests on an explicit hierarchy of races or civilizations, the opposite of treating unequal group outcomes as discrimination.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Ferry defends colonies as outlets for trade and manufactures, though Kipling's moral tone distrusts gain; inferred.

arm-foreign-insurgents.rationale: The doctrine sought direct rule and tutelage over subject peoples, not backing insurgents; inferred.

intervene-in-bloc.rationale: Kipling's 'savage wars of peace' and Ferry's refusal to withdraw accept forcing outcomes on others, though the allied-bloc framing is anachronistic; inferred.

corporate-influence.rationale: No documented position; inferred as indifferent.

residents-only-property.rationale: Not addressed; adherents ranged across liberal to conservative views. Inferred.

job-guarantee.rationale: It carried no domestic economic programme, so adherents split. Inferred.

democratic-peace.rationale: Mill held despotism legitimate for 'barbarians', so spreading democracy was not the aim; inferred disagreement.

no-duty-to-obey.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine rests on imposed law and order and tutelage under authority.

non-intervention.rationale: The doctrine's core is that advanced states have a right and duty to rule and intervene in less advanced societies.

minority-conspiracy.rationale: Inferred: it justified rule by progress, not by conspiracy claims, though racial hierarchy was common.

abolish-legal-marriage.rationale: Inferred from its conservative, European-institution outlook.

local-production.rationale: Ferry's case treated colonies as outlets for trade and industry, implying production for metropolitan markets. Inferred.

informal-organisation.rationale: Inferred: it relied on states, missions and institutions.

national-law-over-international.rationale: Inferred: it held the law of 'civilized' states above the customs of subject peoples.

religious-nation.rationale: Religion was one vehicle of uplift, but the republican and liberal strands were secular. Split.

deference-to-leading-power.rationale: Inferred from its hierarchy of civilizations and the duty of superior powers, but tribute and ritual are not stated.

regional-revenue-retention.rationale: Ferry justified colonies as economic outlets for the metropole, so colonial revenue was not to be kept regionally.

personal-possessions-private.rationale: Inferred from the liberal and bourgeois case for property and trade in Mill and Ferry.

defeat-communism.rationale: Anachronistic: communism as a rival system postdates the doctrine's classic statements, and adherents' views followed their party.

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: No settled position; adherents ranged across liberal and conservative views on public provision.

religion-illusion.rationale: Spreading Christianity was a stated aim of the civilizing mission.

capitalism-progressive.rationale: Inferred from the stage-of-civilization view of progress that Mill and Ferry share; capitalism itself is not discussed.

women-equality-needs-economic-change.rationale: Inferred: no stated position, but its nineteenth-century adherents held conventional views of gender roles.

socialized-care.rationale: Inferred from nineteenth-century adherents' conventional view of family and private care.

purge-loanwords.rationale: Inferred: Macaulay expected English to enrich native languages, not purge them.

treaties-binding.rationale: Inferred from tutelary rule in Ferry and Kipling, where the ruling power sets terms for subject peoples.

cooperative-communities.rationale: Inferred: its aim was remaking societies on European models, not communal self-government.

majority-settlement.rationale: Inferred from its assimilationist model and settler colonialism, though not stated as a policy.

neither-capitalism-nor-communism.rationale: Inferred: adherents defended liberal or conservative orders and rejected radical alternatives.

historical-land-claim.rationale: The case rests on advanced societies' duty to uplift others, not on a people's historical tie to a land; inferred.

holocaust-denial.rationale: The doctrine predates the Holocaust and its Victorian and French adherents rested on claims of progress; inferred that an adherent would reject denial.

criminalize-homosexuality.rationale: Its standard of civilisation included European morality and law, and colonial codes criminalised it (Macaulay's Indian Penal Code); inferred.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Mill defends despotism over 'barbarians' if it improves them (s4), and imperial rule suppressed colonial opposition.

punish-blasphemy.rationale: Macaulay's secular education plan and Mill's liberal tutelage did not centre punishing blasphemy; missionaries differed. Inferred.

colonies-serve-metropole.rationale: Ferry states plainly that colonies provide outlets for the metropole's industry, alongside the duty to civilise.

defensive-jihad-duty.rationale: Jihad has no place in the doctrine, and it was the colonised who invoked it against the mission; inferred.

unreligious-rulers-fought.rationale: Not a doctrine of religious-law rule; the mission set European law and education as the standard. Inferred.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Mill and Macaulay support rule by tutors, not self-rule by subjects, so direct participation was denied in colonies; inferred.

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: The doctrine assumed a hierarchy of races or civilisations (s1, s2), so it did not see oppressions as overlapping; anachronistic.

gender-identity-recognition.rationale: Anachronistic; the doctrine's conventional morals oppose this. Inferred.

assisted-dying.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from conventional moral outlook.

left-right-obsolete.rationale: Anachronistic; the doctrine held the Western order as the standard, not a blend of left and right.

alienated-labor.rationale: Its adherents praised commerce and industry as civilising (s2), so a critique of alienation is not their frame; inferred.

islam-incompatible.rationale: The mission set non-Western societies as in need of uplift, and Kipling and Macaulay cast other cultures as inferior; inferred for Islam.

divine-source-of-authority.rationale: Kipling's and Ferry's cases rest on a Christian or secular duty to civilise, and adherents differed on religion.

religious-dress-in-state.rationale: Anachronistic; assimilationists and secularists would favour it, paternalists less so. Inferred.

social-market-economy.rationale: The doctrine carries no domestic programme (scope), so adherents ranged across economic positions.

abolish-armed-forces.rationale: The doctrine was backed by armed force and conquest (s1, s2); inferred.

rich-first.rationale: The tutelage idea has advanced societies leading and others following step by step (s4), a loose parallel; inferred.

stay-neutral-between-blocs.rationale: Ferry argued that France must expand and hold a rank among powers (s2), so staying out of rivalries does not fit; inferred.

dynastic-succession.rationale: The doctrine's statements concern other peoples, not the form of the colonizers' own government; Britain and France had both monarchies and republics, so adherents split.

interest-free-mutual-credit.rationale: The doctrine carried no domestic economic programme and its liberal-market lean suggests ordinary banks; inferred.

refuse-lender-austerity.rationale: Ferry framed colonies as markets and investment outlets, so imperial lenders' terms would be accepted; inferred.

property-franchise.rationale: Mill and other liberal imperialists tied the vote to education and capacity, which tends toward qualified franchises; inferred.

domination-women-nature.rationale: The mission prized mastering nature through technology and held conventional gender roles, though Mill argued for women's equality; inferred and mixed.

reification.rationale: A Marxist concept foreign to the doctrine, whose proponents defended commerce and property.

press-owned-by-wealth.rationale: Liberal imperialists such as Mill defended press freedom as real in itself and did not argue that private ownership hollows it; inferred.

promulgated-standing-laws.rationale: Macaulay's push for codified law and Ferry's presentation of order and justice as gifts to colonies support government under fixed laws, even though colonial rule itself was often discretionary.

racial-franchise.rationale: The doctrine placed rule in the hands of the civilised race and excluded colonial subjects from government, as the hierarchy of races in s1 and Kipling describes.

online-participation.rationale: Anachronistic; the doctrine says nothing about internet participation.

open-government-data.rationale: Colonial administrations were generally not transparent, but the doctrine does not address publishing records; adherents' views are indeterminate.

interfaith-marriage-restriction.rationale: Missionary Christianity was part of the civilizing project, but liberal adherents resisted legal marriage restrictions; inferred.

boycott-minority-shops.rationale: Targeting a minority's businesses contradicts the doctrine's claim to uplift all subjects under one benevolent rule; inferred.

citizens-assembly.rationale: The doctrine rests on tutelage by an educated elite, as in Mill's argument for guided rule of backward peoples, so decisions by lot-chosen ordinary citizens cut against it. Inferred.

reinterpret-religion.rationale: Civilizers pressed colonized societies to reform customs and law judged barbarous, as Macaulay did in India, which implies reworking inherited religious rulings by reason. Inferred.

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine has no stated view on domestic wealth; Victorian liberals and imperial conservatives, who both held it, split on the question.

open-lgbt-military-service.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine predates the issue, and its Victorian-era adherents upheld conventional morality as part of the civilization they exported.

state-promotes-atheism.rationale: Inferred: the mission promoted religion, above all Christianity, as one of its stated aims, so state atheist education runs against it.

abolish-police-prisons.rationale: Inferred: Ferry and Kipling justify rule by order and force ('savage wars of peace'), so abolishing police and prisons is far from it.

power-sharing-divided-societies.rationale: Inferred: Mill and Ferry treat government as the work of the advanced, not a bargain among communities; the colonial rulers kept executive power to themselves.

charity-over-state-aid.rationale: Inferred: missionary charity and voluntary societies were a main vehicle of the civilizing project, but adherents did not oppose state action at home.

term-limits.rationale: Inferred: Ferry was a career parliamentarian and the doctrine valued experienced elite administrators; no source states a view on term limits.

vote-delegation.rationale: Inferred: Mill and Macaulay favour rule by the educated and an intermediary class, not direct popular control of each policy area.

existential-risk-priority.rationale: Inferred: the issue is anachronistic for a nineteenth-century doctrine, which did not discuss extinction risk.

women-in-religious-leadership.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine carried Victorian Christian and European norms, under which clerical offices were held by men; it took no stated position.

shared-marital-authority.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine exported Victorian family norms, in which the husband was head of the household; it took no stated position.

foreign-residents-local-vote.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine concerns ruling subject peoples and does not address residents' rights; settler and metropolitan citizenship was jealously guarded.

rent-control.rationale: Inferred: it carries no housing programme, and its liberal and imperial backers generally favoured property rights.

abolish-ip.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine says nothing on intellectual property, and the imperial powers that held it were property-protecting.

uniformed-youth.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine has no domestic programme; Kipling-era empire did produce youth movements, but they were not part of the doctrine.

no-nuclear-weapons-on-territory.rationale: Anachronistic: nuclear weapons postdate the doctrine, and nothing in the sources allows an inference.

no-foreign-bases.rationale: Inferred: imperial powers established garrisons and bases in subject lands, so hosting foreign forces is at odds with the logic of rule by the advanced; the doctrine itself says nothing.

recognise-genocide.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine downplays or excuses colonial violence as part of uplift, so adherents would not favour formal recognition.

income-for-work-not-ownership.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine concerns empire rather than domestic distribution, and its liberal and conservative proponents differed.

never-kill-self-defence.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine defends the use of force to rule and uplift others, so it does not hold killing wrong in defence of others.

unbroken-national-continuity.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine ranks civilisations by stage of development and does not claim unbroken ancient continuity for any nation.

sex-socially-constructed.rationale: Anachronistic: the nineteenth-century doctrine predates this theory and its naturalised hierarchies assume fixed sex roles.

no-fixed-category-of-women.rationale: Anachronistic: the doctrine predates this question, and its hierarchy of fixed categories points against it.

martyrs-honoured.rationale: Inferred: imperial culture honoured those who died in its service, as in Kipling's call to duty, but the doctrine itself does not address it.

politics-spiritual-struggle.rationale: Inferred: Ferry and Mill justify empire by progress, education and trade rather than as a spiritual struggle, though Kipling and missionary strands add religion.

homeland-cultural-centre.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine centres on the metropolitan power spreading its culture abroad, not on a homeland serving a diaspora.

culture-before-state.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine joins cultural uplift with state rule, and the sources show no ranking of one over the other.

god-not-male.rationale: Inferred: the missionary and imperial context assumed a male God, though the sources do not address it.

scripture-judged-by-women.rationale: Anachronistic: the doctrine predates this idea and held to a hierarchy that did not use women's full humanity as a test.

economy-in-majority-hands.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine gives the colonizing power control over the colony's economy and trade, as Ferry's speech argues; the statement is about nations rather than empires, so only a weak match.

single-unit-for-people.rationale: Inferred: imperial powers drew colonial borders to suit their own rule, not to group peoples, and the doctrine does not call for this.

independent-unions.rationale: Imperial rule was top-down and the doctrine had no labour programme; adherents were mostly sceptical of independent unions. Inferred.

socialism-needs-workers-power.rationale: The doctrine rests on elite tutelage and hierarchy, not workers' power. Inferred.

local-essentials-public.rationale: No documented position; adherents ranged from liberals to conservatives. Inferred.

second-chamber.rationale: The doctrine has no constitutional programme; adherents followed their home institutions. Inferred.

municipal-property.rationale: The mission promoted trade, private law and metropolitan state authority, not communal ownership. Inferred.

confederal-coordination.rationale: Colonial rule was centralised under the metropole, and delegates without decision power over local assemblies does not match its model of tutelage. Inferred.

family-wage.rationale: Victorian and French imperial adherents broadly held the male-breadwinner household ideal. Inferred.

faster-drug-approval.rationale: Anachronistic; the doctrine addresses medicine only as public health abroad (s1). Inferred.

anonymous-payments.rationale: Anachronistic; the doctrine favours state control and supervision of subjects' exchange. Inferred.

person-over-state.rationale: Mill allows despotism over 'barbarians' if the end is their improvement, treating persons as means to a civilizing end for the societies concerned.

spiritual-nature.rationale: Spreading religion alongside education and law is a stated aim of the mission, and Kipling frames it as a moral duty.

regional-powers-revocable.rationale: Colonial administration kept powers with the metropole and could revoke any local autonomy. Inferred.

racial-group-interests.rationale: Ferry asserts superior races' duties over inferior ones, but adherents spoke of duty and the nation's interests rather than organising racial groups to defend interests; split. Inferred.

racial-pride.rationale: Ferry and Kipling assume the superiority of the colonizing race or civilization and take pride in it. Inferred from s2 and s3.

defensive-wars-only.rationale: Ferry demands expansion, naval bases and refusal to withdraw, and Kipling calls it 'savage wars of peace', so force is used to conquer, not just defend.

language-defines-nation.rationale: Inferred from the assimilationist model, which spread the colonizer's language and culture across peoples rather than recognizing nations by shared language.

communal-electorates.rationale: Inferred: the British protective model kept native communities distinct, while the French assimilationist model rejected it, so adherents split.

foreign-partition-plot.rationale: Inferred: adherents saw their own powers as dominant and expanding, not as threatened with partition.

free-public-college.rationale: Inferred from Macaulay's Minute, which favoured educating a small elite rather than mass schooling.

pollution-taxes.rationale: Inferred: nothing in the doctrine addresses pollution, and its liberal and conservative adherents favoured industrial expansion.

future-generations.rationale: The doctrine is about duty to other peoples; adherents had no common line on duties to future generations.

women-distinct-values.rationale: Inferred from the 19th-century hierarchies the doctrine shared, which gave women little public role.

arms-reduction.rationale: Inferred from its dependence on military force to extend and hold colonial rule.

open-diplomacy.rationale: Inferred from imperial practice: Ferry's speech was addressed to a chamber but colonial and alliance diplomacy was routinely secret.

capital-controls.rationale: Ferry argued colonies were needed as outlets for French capital and trade, so free movement of capital abroad was part of the case.

state-arms-monopoly.rationale: Inferred: colonial rule rested on a monopoly of force by the imperial state, but sources do not discuss disarmament.

soldiers-refuse-war.rationale: Kipling presents imperial service and 'savage wars of peace' as duty, and Ferry insists on keeping the empire's forces committed.

collective-bargaining.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine has no domestic labour programme; adherents ranged from liberals to conservatives.

in-work-tax-credits.rationale: Inferred: no domestic programme, so adherents split by party.

fiscal-rules-binding.rationale: Inferred: no domestic fiscal doctrine is attached to the civilizing mission.

restructure-world-economy.rationale: Ferry presents colonies as economic outlets for the metropole's industry, so the doctrine favours the colonizer's economic interest, not remaking world rules for poorer peoples.

smash-state-machine.rationale: Inferred: Macaulay and Mill propose using the imperial state's law and schools to uplift subjects, not demolishing it.

free-economic-experiment.rationale: Inferred: it prescribes a single model of civilization for subject peoples, which is opposed to letting communities choose.

nature-as-capital.rationale: Inferred: Ferry values colonies for raw materials and markets, but valuing nature as capital is not discussed.

sacred-nation.rationale: Ferry ties France's rank and greatness among nations to its imperial duty, treating the nation as an enduring mission.

student-debt-relief.rationale: Inferred: no domestic programme, and student loans did not exist in the period.

internal-colonialism.rationale: Inferred: adherents defended colonial rule as uplift, and would likely reject describing domestic regional inequality as colonial exploitation.

shared-human-nature.rationale: Ferry speaks of superior and inferior races and Kipling calls subjects 'half-devil and half-child', rejecting equal shared nature.

public-service-media.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine predates broadcasting and has no media programme.

religions-one-truth.rationale: Ferry, Kipling and Macaulay treat native religions and learning as inferior to the colonizer's; mission Christianity was part of the uplift, so one shared truth is not accepted.

farm-price-support.rationale: Inferred from Mill's liberal political economy and Ferry's trade-driven case for empire; the doctrine has no domestic farm programme.

keep-nuclear-weapons.rationale: Anachronistic: the doctrine predates nuclear weapons and gives no principle to infer from.

workers-own-party.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine was voiced by governing elites, and Ferry also defends empire as an answer to social unrest at home.

ban-fgm.rationale: Inferred: the mission justified rule partly by suppressing customs it called barbarous, which would support a ban; the sources do not name FGM.

women-property-inheritance.rationale: The doctrine carried no stance on women's property, and its leading voices disagreed on women's legal status.

one-language-many-names.rationale: A linguistic classification question the doctrine never addresses.

pollution-tort-liability.rationale: Anachronistic: environmental liability is not discussed by the sources and nothing in the doctrine implies a view.

customary-chiefs-lawmaking.rationale: Split by model: the assimilationist strand rejects customary authority, while the paternal strand ruled through native chiefs.

environment-over-liberty.rationale: Inferred: the doctrine prizes progress, trade and development as the measure of civilization, and has no environmental theme.

mandatory-sentences.rationale: The doctrine has no domestic penal programme; Mill's liberal case for discretion and Kipling's paternal order point opposite ways.

immigrants-learn-language.rationale: Inferred from the assimilationist model, which expects subjects to adopt the ruler's language and learning, as Macaulay urged for English in India.

no-compulsory-union.rationale: The doctrine has no labour-law programme, so no position on compulsory union membership can be drawn from it.

voter-id.rationale: Mill's tutelage logic and the paternal model favour restricting political participation to the educated, which suggests tolerating ID and citizenship gates; inferred, not stated.

religious-equal-recognition.rationale: The mission usually carried the colonizer's own (often missionary) religion as the standard of civilization, so equal legal footing for rival faiths was not its aim; inferred from s1.

democracy-is-procedure.rationale: Rule is justified as tutelage until peoples are fit for self-government, so legitimacy rests on improvement, not on elections; inferred from Mill and Ferry.

premarital-sex.rationale: Spreading European moral and religious norms was part of the uplift, and Victorian-era norms condemned sex outside marriage; inferred.

internet-shutdowns.rationale: A paternal, order-first colonial state would accept cutting communications for order, though the technology postdates the doctrine; inferred.

negative-income-tax.rationale: The doctrine predates cash-transfer schemes and favours state-directed uplift and market discipline over unconditional payments; inferred.

women-suffrage.rationale: Adherents were split and the texts are silent: Mill backed women's suffrage while Ferry and Kipling did not address it.

religion-oppresses-women.rationale: Civilizers often cited native religions and customs as oppressing women to justify intervention, but they credited backwardness generally, not religion as such; inferred.

race-social-construct.rationale: Ferry states openly that superior races have rights over inferior ones, and the doctrine commonly rested on a racial or civilizational hierarchy, so racial categories were treated as real.

gender-equality-agencies.rationale: The doctrine carried no programme of equality machinery, and gender-equality agencies are a late twentieth-century device; inferred.

homestead-ownership.rationale: Inferred: colonial rule often justified taking 'unused' land as a way of putting it to productive use, but the doctrine states no property theory.

international-criminal-courts.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from its view that advanced states hold authority over lesser peoples and are not themselves judged by outside bodies.

scripture-inerrant.rationale: Inferred: it spread Christianity as one of its tools, but Mill and Ferry were secular, so adherents split.

gendered-self-government.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from the hierarchical, paternal tutelage model with no stated view on gender equality in self-government.

defend-planned-state.rationale: Inferred: its backers were capitalist, liberal and conservative imperial states and not planned economies.

indirect-election.rationale: Inferred: no stated position, and adherents ranged from liberals to conservatives.

national-church-status.rationale: Inferred: no stated view; its adherents included both established-church and secular republican supporters.

minority-territorial-autonomy.rationale: Inferred: the assimilation model sought to remake subjects, not grant autonomy, though the paternal model sometimes preserved native rule.

disputed-territory-plebiscite.rationale: Inferred: the metropole decided the fate of territories, not their inhabitants' votes.

keep-colonial-borders.rationale: Inferred: it justified rule, not independence, so the question arises only after the doctrine's end.

simple-living.rationale: Inferred: it championed commerce, technology and progress as the gifts of civilization.

restrict-indigenous-settlement.rationale: Inferred: the paternal model protected native society while the assimilation model encouraged settlement, so it was split.

equal-conscription.rationale: Anachronistic; inferred from Victorian-era gender roles, with no stated position.

homeland-spiritual-bond.rationale: Rule was justified as uplifting subjects, not as a spiritual tie between a people and land; inferred from the tutelage rationale, and colonizers treated colonial land as a resource to develop.

extrajudicial-killing.rationale: Nothing in the doctrine addresses drug policy; its rule-of-law and legal-reform emphasis (Ferry, Macaulay) suggests trial over summary killing, though colonial rule often used harsh force. Inferred.

close-ties-china.rationale: The doctrine is about European and Western powers ruling others, so alignment with an Asian power is inferred as unfavoured; it never addressed China directly.

protect-kin-minorities.rationale: The doctrine concerns rulers of other peoples, not diaspora minorities; settler-colonial and protective-empire strands pulled in different directions. Inferred.

resources-common-ownership.rationale: Mill and Ferry defended property and trade-led development, so equal common ownership of resources is inferred as unfavoured; not stated.

self-ownership.rationale: Mill's harm principle favours self-ownership for the civilized, yet the doctrine denied it to subject peoples and allowed forced labour in practice; adherents split.

cut-consumption-tax.rationale: Fiscal policy is not part of the doctrine; adherents followed their home parties. Inferred as neutral.

targeted-social-spending.rationale: Social spending design is outside the doctrine; adherents ranged from liberals to conservatives and republicans.

bypass-parties-groups.rationale: Colonial administration ran through official hierarchies and Ferry defended parliamentary France; bypassing parties is not part of the doctrine, so mildly disagree. Inferred.

no-business-privileges.rationale: Mill and Ferry tied empire to free trade, but colonies were also run through chartered and favoured firms, so adherents are split toward mild disagreement. Inferred.

no-denominational-politics.rationale: Missionary Christianity and secular republican assimilation both claimed the mission, and administrators often governed through religious communities; adherents split.

tech-with-ancestral-values.rationale: The mission held that advanced modern civilization should replace native custom, as in Macaulay's Minute dismissing native learning (s5), so a return to ancestral values is inferred as rejected.

wife-divorce-without-consent.rationale: Ferry and Kipling framed reform of 'barbarous' native custom as part of the mission, so wives' right to divorce is inferred as favoured; colonial law often left personal law alone, so only low confidence.

national-resource-control.rationale: Colonial powers extracted resources under metropolitan control, so national control by the subject country is inferred as opposed; the doctrine did not address it directly.

distribution-by-process.rationale: The doctrine has no distribution theory; Victorian liberals like Mill leaned toward process-based fairness while paternalists did not. Inferred.

financial-transactions-tax.rationale: Ferry framed empire as an economic outlet for trade and capital, which implies hostility to taxes on cross-border trade. Anachronistic; inferred from s2.

racism-not-main-obstacle.rationale: The question is anachronistic: the doctrine openly assumed racial hierarchy and tutelage, so it had no modern view on racism as an obstacle. Inferred.

unjust-law-not-binding.rationale: Anachronistic and split: Macaulay's legal reform and natural-law traditions coexisted with positivist colonial codes. Inferred.

automate-paid-work.rationale: Anachronistic; the doctrine praised technology as part of what it spread (s1) but never addressed automation or shorter work. Inferred.

multipolar-world.rationale: Ferry and Kipling cast the imperial powers as the carriers of civilization over subject peoples, which leans toward a hierarchy of powers rather than independent centres. Inferred.

labour-theory-of-value.rationale: Ferry grounded empire in markets and commercial outlets rather than labour as the source of value. Inferred from s2.

patriotism-serves-workers.rationale: Ferry tied empire to national greatness and to working-class prosperity, but the doctrine had no worker-focused politics and adherents followed their home party. Inferred.

material-over-identity.rationale: The doctrine addresses empire, not left strategy, so the statement does not apply; adherents ranged across parties. Inferred.

market-under-party-rule.rationale: Nothing in the sources addresses communist party rule; as a European and American imperial doctrine it opposed it. Inferred.

missingStatements.text: Peoples who are not yet capable of governing themselves should not be given self-government until they have been educated for it.
missingStatements.rationale: Mill limits liberty to peoples capable of free discussion, and Ferry and Kipling treat rule as a stage before readiness.

missingStatements.text: European languages and learning should replace native languages and learning as the medium of education in colonies.
missingStatements.rationale: Macaulay's Minute defends English-medium education and dismisses native literature, the assimilationist model recorded in s1.

notes: Strands differ: assimilationist (Ferry, Macaulay) versus associationist or protective (some French and British colonial administrators); racial-hierarchy versus stage-of-civilization justifications; and modern uses of the label by critics, who apply it to development aid or rights-promotion. Domestic-policy answers are inferences with no stated adherent position.
